statement: If there be two pyramids of the same height which have triangular bases, and cach of them be divided into two pyramids equal to one another and similar to the whole, and into two equal prisms, then, as the base of the one pyramid is to the base of the other pyramid, so will all the prisms in the one pyramid be to all the prisms, being equal in multitude, in the other pyramid.
heath_proof: Let there be two pyramids of the same height which have the triangular bases ABC, DEF, and vertices the points G, H, and let each of them be divided into two pyramids equal to one another and similar to the whole and into two equal prisms; [XII. 3] I say that, as the base ABC is to the base DEF, so are all the prisms in the pyramid ABCG to all the prisms, being equal in multitude, in the pyramid DEFH, For, since BO is equal to OC, and AL to LC, therefore LO is parallel to AB, and the triangle ABC is similar to the triangle LOC. For the same reason the triangle DEF is also similar to the triangle RVF. And, since BC is double of CO, and EF of FV, therefore, as BC is to CO, so is EF to FV. And on BC, CO are described the similar and similarly situated rectilineal figures ABC, LOC, and on EF, FV the similar and similarly situated figures DEF, RVF; therefore, as the triangle ABC is to the triangle LOC, so is the triangle DEF to the triangle RVF; [VI. 22] therefore, alternately, as the triangle ABC is to the triangle DEF, so is the triangle LOC to the triangle RVF. [V. 16] But, as the triangle LOC is to the triangle RVF, so is the prism in which the triangle LOC is the base and PMN its opposite to the prism in which the triangle RVF is the base and STU its opposite; [Lemma following]therefore also, as the triangle ABC is to the triangle DEF, so is the prism in which the triangle LOC is the base and PMN its opposite to the prism in which the triangle RVF is the base and STU its opposite. But, as the said prisms are to one another, so is the prism in which the parallelogram KBOL is the base and the straight line PM its opposite to the prism in which the parallelogram QEVR is the base and the straight line ST its opposite. [XI. 39; cf. XII. 3] Therefore also the two prisms, that in which the parallelogram KBOL is the base and PM its opposite, and that in which the triangle LOC is the base and PMN its opposite, are to the prisms in which QEVR is the base and the straight line ST its opposite and in which the triangle RVF is the base and STU its opposite in the same ratio [V. 12] Therefore also, as the base ABC is to the base DEF, so are the said two prisms to the said two prisms. And similarly, if the pyramids PMNG, STUH be divided into two prisms and two pyramids, as the base PMN is to the base STU, so will the two prisms in the pyramid PMNG be to the two prisms in the pyramid STUH. But, as the base PMN is to the base STU, so is the base ABC to the base DEF; for the triangles PMN, STU are equal to the triangles LOC, RVF respectively. Therefore also, as the base ABC is to the base DEF, so are the four prisms to the four prisms. And similarly also, if we divide the remaining pyramids into two pyramids and into two prisms, then, as the base ABC is to the base DEF, so will all the prisms in the pyramid ABCG be to all the prisms, being equal in multitude, in the pyramid DEFH.

12.4
**Statement:** If there be two pyramids of the same height which have triangular bases, and cach of them be divided into two pyramids equal to one another and similar to the whole, and into two equal prisms, then, as the base of the one pyramid is to the base of the other pyramid, so will all the prisms in the one pyramid be to all the prisms, being equal in multitude, in the other pyramid.

**Step 1.** Let the two pyramids be D–ABC and D′–A′B′C′, with common height h. Bisect their edges (1.10). In the first pyramid, let E, F, G, H, I, K be the respective midpoints of AB, BC, CA, DA, DB, DC, and use corresponding primed letters in the second. Make the midpoint division of 12.3: the smaller pyramids are D–HIK and I–BEF, while the prisms have triangular ends AEG, HIK and EFI, GCK. Denote these prisms by R and S, and the corresponding primed prisms by R′ and S′. Thus R = S and R′ = S′ (12.3). We shall compare prisms by completing them to parallelepipeds, so that the equal-height comparison of 11.32 applies directly.

**Step 2.** The midpoint parallels give HI ∥ AB and HK ∥ AC (6.2); consequently the planes HIK and ABC are parallel (11.15). Draw DO perpendicular to the plane ABC (11.11), and let N be its intersection with the plane HIK. Relabel the base vertices if necessary so that O ≠ A. The plane DAO cuts the two parallel planes in AO and HN, so HN ∥ AO (11.16). Hence, in triangle DAO, DN:NO = DH:HA (6.2). Since DH = HA, the section bisects the perpendicular height: DN = NO = h/2. The same argument applies to the primed pyramid.

**Step 3.** The line DO is perpendicular to HIK as well: intersect the parallel planes with two planes through DO, use their parallel traces and corresponding right angles, and then apply the criterion for perpendicularity to a plane (11.16, 1.29, 11.4). Moreover, perpendicular segments between two parallel planes are equal: such segments are parallel (11.6), and their endpoint joins are parallel (11.16), so they are opposite sides of a parallelogram (1.34). It follows that R and R′ have equal height h/2. Both smaller pyramids in each original pyramid also have height h/2: D–HIK has altitude DN, while I–BEF has its vertex in HIK and its base in ABC (D6.4).

**Step 4.** Write a = [ABC], a′ = [A′B′C′], b = [AEG], and b′ = [A′E′G′], where brackets denote triangular areas. Since AB = 2AE, triangles ABG and AEG, having the same altitude to AB, satisfy [ABG] = 2b (6.1). Likewise, AC = 2AG gives a = 2[ABG] (6.1). Thus a = 4b, and similarly a′ = 4b′ (CN2). Therefore a:a′ = b:b′, since equimultiples have the same ratio as the original magnitudes (5.15). This uses the equal-altitude triangle comparison directly, without a duplicate-ratio calculation.

**Step 5.** Complete the triangular ends of R to corresponding parallelograms, obtaining a parallelepiped T; do the same for R′, obtaining T′ (1.31). These completions retain the respective heights of the prisms. If c and c′ are their base areas, then c = 2b and c′ = 2b′, since a diagonal bisects a parallelogram (1.34). The plane through the corresponding base diagonals bisects each parallelepiped, with R and R′ as the respective halves; hence T = 2R and T′ = 2R′ (11.28).

**Step 6.** The parallelepipeds T and T′ have equal height by Step 3. Therefore T:T′ = c:c′ (11.32). Removing the equal multiplicities on both sides gives R:R′ = b:b′ (5.15, 5.11). Combining this with Step 4 yields R:R′ = a:a′ (5.11).

**Step 7.** Since S = R and S′ = R′ (12.3), the two prism totals are respectively 2R and 2R′. Consequently (R + S):(R′ + S′) = R:R′ = a:a′ (5.15). Thus the required assertion holds for the two prisms of each first division.

**Step 8.** The bases of the smaller pyramids retain the same comparison. Indeed, [HIK] = [AEG] = b, since these are the opposite triangular ends of the prism R (D11.13). Also, applying 6.1 twice to the midpoints E and F gives [ABC] = 4[BEF], just as in Step 4; hence [BEF] = b. The corresponding primed bases likewise both equal b′. Each corresponding pair of smaller pyramids therefore has bases in the ratio a:a′ (5.15), and has equal height h/2 by Step 3.

**Step 9.** If the division is repeated, apply Steps 1–7 separately to each corresponding pair of remaining pyramids. Step 8 preserves the base ratio a:a′, and Step 3 preserves equality of the corresponding heights. Thus, at every finite corresponding repetition, each newly obtained prism is to its counterpart as a is to a′. This follows by repeating the already established prism comparison, using the divisions supplied by 12.3.

**Step 10.** Enumerate all the prisms obtained in the two corresponding finite subdivisions as V₁, …, Vₘ and V′₁, …, V′ₘ. By Steps 6–9, every ratio Vᵢ:V′ᵢ equals a:a′. Therefore the sum of the antecedents is to the sum of the consequents in that same ratio (5.12):
(V₁ + ··· + Vₘ):(V′₁ + ··· + V′ₘ) = a:a′ = [ABC]:[A′B′C′].
Hence, as the base of one pyramid is to the base of the other, so are all the prisms in the one to all the corresponding prisms, equal in multitude, in the other. This includes the original two-prism divisions and proves the proposition.
